readerTitle: How deep should you go into a new country?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장기계 제조사, 치과용 예약 소프트웨어) + 실제 연구 (Uppsala 모델, 국제 신생기업 연구)
insight: 시장 진입 방식은 '통제'와 '투입' 사이의 사다리다. 수요를 아직 모를 때는 이기는 핵심을 지킬 수 있는 가장 가벼운 칸에서 시작하고, 배우면서 한 칸씩 올라간다.
misconception: 해외에 제대로 진출하려면 처음부터 현지 법인과 사무실을 세워야 한다. 반대로 소프트웨어는 온라인으로 팔리니 진입 방식을 고민할 필요가 없다.

sources.text: Johanson, J., & Vahlne, J.-E. (1977). The Internationalization Process of the Firm. Journal of International Business Studies.
Oviatt, B. M., & McDougall, P. P. (1994). Toward a Theory of International New Ventures. Journal of International Business Studies.
국제경영의 표준 개념 (수출, 라이선싱·프랜차이징, 합작투자, 단독 자회사)

factChecks.note: Uppsala 모델 설명(스웨덴 기업들이 비정기 수출 → 대리인 → 판매 자회사 → 현지 생산 순으로 단계적으로 진출하고, 시장 지식이 늘수록 투입을 늘린다는 관찰)이 1977년 논문 내용과 맞는지 원문으로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연구 대상 기업 수 등 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.
Oviatt & McDougall(1994)의 '국제 신생기업(international new ventures)' 개념을 카드에서 '창업 초기부터 여러 나라에서 파는 회사'로 단순화했습니다. 표현이 과하지 않은지 확인하세요.
포장기계 제조사와 치과 예약 소프트웨어 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 특정 국가의 데이터 보관·세무 규정은 일반론으로만 언급했고 법률 조언이 아님을 유지하세요.

cards.title: How deep should you go into a new country?
body: Two companies want customers in the same new country. One makes packaging machines that weigh two tonnes. The other sells software that weighs nothing.
Both face the same question, and it isn't *whether* to go. It's how much to put on the ground, and how soon.

image.label: A heavy machine crate and a laptop at the same border gate
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 국경 게이트 앞에 커다란 나무 상자(기계)와 노트북이 나란히 서 있음. 게이트 너머에 '작은 가판대 → 사무실 → 공장'처럼 점점 커지는 건물 세 개가 계단처럼 배치. 실제 국기·로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your first market abroad.
body: You make packaging machines for food factories. A few buyers in a large new country have asked for quotes, but you don't know how big demand really is.
Your edge at home is fast repairs: a broken machine stops a whole production line. How do you enter?

options.text: Build a local assembly plant and sales office to show you're serious
options.feedback: You'd get full control and buyer trust, but you'd bet millions before knowing if demand exists. Undoing a factory is slow and costly.

options.text: Sell through a local distributor and train its technicians to do your repairs
options.feedback: You spend little while you learn the market, and you protect the one thing you win on: service. The cost is sharing margin and the customer relationship.

options.text: License your design to a local manufacturer for a royalty
options.feedback: Cheap and quick, with income from day one. But you hand over your know-how and lose control of quality and repairs, the very thing your name rests on.

cards.title: Entry modes: a ladder of control
body: An **entry mode** is how you set up shop in a new market. The common options form a ladder.
Each step up gives you more control over price, quality and customers. It also asks for more money, more people and more commitment, and it's harder to walk back.

cards.title: Same ladder, different first step.
body: For the machine maker, even exporting is expensive: freight, import duties and repairs far from home. Its first question is who fixes machines locally.

For a software company, the bottom rung is almost free. Foreign customers can sign up online tomorrow. Its real question is what must exist *locally* to keep them: language, local payment methods, support in their time zone, sometimes data stored in the country.
Different products, one test: what does a customer here need that you can't deliver from home?

image.label: Two ladders side by side, one starting high, one starting at ground level
image.brief: 사다리 두 개를 나란히. 왼쪽(기계 상자 아이콘)은 첫 칸부터 무거운 짐을 짊어진 모습, 오른쪽(노트북 아이콘)은 첫 칸을 가볍게 밟고 있지만 위쪽 칸에 '언어', '결제', '지원', '데이터' 라벨 표지판. 로고 없음.

cards.title: Many firms climb one rung at a time.
body: In 1977, researchers Jan Johanson and Jan-Erik Vahlne studied how Swedish companies went abroad. Many followed a pattern: occasional exports, then local agents, then their own sales office, and only later local production.
Their explanation: **commitment grows with knowledge**. Each rung teaches you about the market, which makes the next, bigger bet less risky.
Later research found exceptions. Some young firms sell in many countries from the start, especially when the product travels easily, like software.

cards.title: Light modes have hidden costs.
body: A licensee or partner learns your methods and can become your competitor. A distributor often owns the customer relationship, and buying it back later can be expensive.
Going slowly has a price too. While you test, a local rival can lock up the best customers.
So the lightest rung isn't always right. Pick the lightest one that still protects what makes you win.

cards.title: Now it's appointment software for dentists.
body: Your scheduling software sells to dental clinics at home. Lately, clinics in a neighboring country sign up on their own, with no marketing. But many cancel within two months. They say support is only in your language, and invoices don't match local formats.

options.text: Open a local office with a 15-person sales team
options.feedback: You'd gain control and speed, but you'd scale sales before fixing why clinics leave. More sign-ups would just mean more cancellations.

options.text: Localize invoices and support, and test a reseller deal with a dental supply firm that already visits clinics
options.feedback: You fix what's breaking and borrow a trusted local channel at low cost. You give up some margin and must keep the reseller's service quality in check.

options.text: Change nothing; the sign-ups are free growth
options.feedback: It costs nothing, and demand is clearly real. But the cancellations show that exporting alone isn't enough for these customers.

cards.title: Enter on the lightest rung that protects your edge.
body: Entry modes trade control for commitment. Start where you can learn cheaply without giving away what makes you win, then climb as you learn.
**Try it today:** for a market you're eyeing, write down the one thing customers there must get from you. Then ask which rung is the lowest that still delivers it.
